newsitem.title: INDIA: Separatist movements strain Indian unity.
newsitem.headline: Separatist movements strain Indian unity.

text.p: Bombs in the northeast, blasts in Kashmir, explosions in the capital -- India begins its 50th year of independence confronting a host of separatist movements tearing at the national fabric.
Freed from British rule in 1947, India has built a modern nation state that encompasses a staggering variety of cultures and religions spread over a sprawling land mass.
But separatist movements haunt the world's second most populous country, claiming lives and creating a centrifugal force that strains the ties which bind the nation.
In the past week, bombs killed more than 40 people in three regions separated by thousands of kilometres (miles) but linked by violent guerrilla movements.
Two blasts on a railway track last Monday tore apart a train in the northeastern state of Assam. The official death toll was 33, although authorities say more were probably killed.
Bodo tribal militants fighting for a separate state inside of Assam claimed responsibility for the blasts.

On Friday a bomb planted in a scooter taxi exploded near the home of the chief minister of troubled Jammu and Kashmir state, killing seven people. The chief minister, Farooq Abdullah, was out of the country.
Jamait-ul-Mujahideen, a militant group fighting for Kashmir to join neighbouring Pakistan, claimed responsibility for the blast, which came two days after a grenade attack on a state junior minister.
On Saturday, two bombs, one in a bus and the other in a taxi, went off in the Indian capital, killing one person and injuring at least 11. No one claimed responsibility.

The attacks were only the latest incidents of violence in a country grappling with insurgencies ranging from Islamic separatists in the Himalayan mountains to Maoist leftists in the southern state of Andhra Pradesh.
Naga tribal militants in Nagaland state, Sikh separatists in Punjab state, Maoist Naxalites in Andhra Pradesh -- all are fighting against New Delhi's rule.
The number of movements reflects India's diversity. Former French president Charles de Gaulle used to point out the difficulty of governing a country with hundreds of cheeses.
Try India, with some 179 languages and 544 dialects, according to a 1925 survey by linguist George Grierson.
"It is a vast country, more a continent," said political analyst Rasheed Talib said. "It is very linguistically and racially varied."
India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, tackled the language challenge, steering the country toward a federal system with state boundaries corresponding roughly to linguistic divisions.

But Talib said the pain of partition, when millions were killed in communal slaughter after mostly Hindu India and Islamic Pakistan were carved out of British India in August 1947, has made India's rulers reluctant to grant substantial autonomy to regions.
"Partition created a trauma in the Indian mind about secessionism," he said. "But people are resorting to violence because they have not been given autonomous political space."
New Delhi's rulers are caught between the need to protect India's hard-fought unity while addressing regional concerns.

Days after he took office in June, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda promised "maximum autonomy" to Jammu and Kashmir state, where more than 20,000 people have been killed since the separatist insurgency erupted in 1990.
Kashmiris are still waiting for an autonomy package.
Talib said: "In the next 50 years, India's main challenge will be whether to let loose the tight hold on the country or proceed in stages to decentralisation."
